meta.description: Frank Lloyd Wright did say a version in 1958 — but he was repeating a doctors' adage in print since 1900, and this wording is Evan Esar's 1968 rewrite.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A Man Is a Fool If He Drinks Before He Reaches Fifty, and a Fool If He Doesn't Drink Afterward'?
meta.ogDescription: Wright said a version of it in 1958. He didn't coin it: the saying was anonymous medical advice in print by 1900, and this exact wording dates from 1968.

answer.label: Not coined by Frank Lloyd Wright — an older doctors’ adage
answer.authorDates: In print by 1900 · quoted by Frank Lloyd Wright in 1958
answer.sourceLine: Wright really did say a version of this out loud — he is quoted delivering it in the New York Times Magazine of 22 June 1958, explaining his single pre-dinner Irish whisky. But he did not invent it: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the same saying in print as anonymous medical advice by 1900, and hypothesises that Wright (like William Faulkner, who used a version of it too) heard it from a doctor. The exact wording asked about here is not Wright’s either: it is the slightly altered form Evan Esar printed under Wright’s name in 20,000 Quips and Quotes in 1968.

source.heading: Where Wright actually said it

docMeta.dd: “A man is a fool if he drinks before he reaches the age of 50, and a fool if he doesn’t afterward.”
“Life Begins at 40 (x 2),” New York Times Magazine, 22 June 1958, p. SM10
Journal of Social Science, no. 38 (December 1900), pp. 127–28 — anonymous: “Some one has said…”
Evan Esar, 20,000 Quips and Quotes (Doubleday, 1968), p. 243 — Wright’s words slightly modified

source.excerpt: Before dinner he often sips a single Irish whisky with a water chaser. “A man is a fool if he drinks before he reaches the age of 50, and a fool if he doesn’t afterward,” he explains.
trail: 1792 — the underlying idea is already in print, with the threshold set at thirty: a Salem, Massachusetts newspaper carries “He who drinks before he is thirty, can take no great pleasure in drinking.” Not yet the saying, but the same reasoning. Quote Investigator ↗

1900 — the earliest known matching form, offered as medical advice at the American Social Science Association’s annual meeting and printed in the Journal of Social Science, no. 38, credited to nobody: “Some one has said, ‘A man is a fool who drinks before he is fifty, and a blank fool who does not do so moderately thereafter.’” The issue at the Internet Archive ↗

1901–1951 — the saying keeps surfacing as doctor’s advice, the threshold sliding between forty and fifty: a 1901 medical journal crediting “the elder Gross”; a 1942 profile of Goodyear co-founder Charles Seiberling quoting his physician; a 1943 Cleveland Plain Dealer profile; a 1951 newspaper column. Quote Investigator ↗

1958, then 1968 — Wright delivers his version to the New York Times Magazine on 22 June 1958, as confirmed by WIST ↗; ten years later Evan Esar reprints it in 20,000 Quips and Quotes with the wording slightly altered, and it is Esar’s sentence, not Wright’s, that the internet quotes today.
source.excerptNote: The 1958 passage as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the New York Times Magazine feature “Life Begins at 40 (x 2)” by Arturo and Janeann Gonzalez. Note that Wright says “the age of 50” and “if he doesn’t afterward” — not the shorter, tidier sentence that now travels under his name. The original article is available only through subscription newspaper archives (ProQuest); the date and wording are independently indexed by WIST ↗.

source.rightsHolder: The New York Times Company (1958 article by Arturo and Janeann Gonzalez); Evan Esar / Doubleday (1968 reworded form)
source.rightsNote: Both documented forms of this sentence are modern publications: Wright’s wording appeared in the New York Times Magazine of 22 June 1958, and the popular wording first appears in Evan Esar’s 20,000 Quips and Quotes (Doubleday, 1968), so the texts shown here are treated as in copyright. The anonymous 1900 form in the Journal of Social Science is long out of copyright — but it is a different sentence, and it is not the one people quote.

author.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
author.kicker: The man who made it famous
author.heading: About Frank Lloyd Wright
author.bio: Frank Lloyd Wright (born Frank Lincoln Wright, 8 June 1867 – 9 April 1959) was the American architect behind Fallingwater, the Guggenheim and the Prairie and Usonian houses — and, in his last decades, a national character as much as a designer, dispensing opinions to reporters with total confidence. This particular opinion, though, he was passing on rather than minting: by the time he offered it to the New York Times Magazine in 1958, the saying had been circulating among American physicians for well over half a century. He is the reason it is famous, not the reason it exists.

misattribution.heading: What the internet gets wrong
misattribution.intro: This line is pinned to Frank Lloyd Wright on every quotation aggregator going, usually with no source. Wright is a genuine part of the story — but two separate things about the popular credit are wrong.

items.why: The saying was already in print as anonymous medical advice in the Journal of Social Science, no. 38 (December 1900): “Some one has said, ‘A man is a fool who drinks before he is fifty, and a blank fool who does not do so moderately thereafter.’” A 1901 medical journal credits “the elder Gross” with a version set at forty. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that Wright heard it from others — conceivably his doctor.

Wright’s documented sentence is “before he reaches the age of 50 … and a fool if he doesn’t afterward.” The shorter form now in circulation — “before he reaches fifty … and a fool if he doesn’t drink afterwards” — is the one Esar printed over Wright’s name in 1968, which Quote Investigator ↗ describes as Wright’s words “slightly modified.”

William Faulkner of Oxford (1965) records the photographer J. R. Cofield recalling Faulkner say: “But a man shouldn’t fool with booze until he’s fifty; then he’s a damnfool if he doesn’t.” Different wording, same borrowed saying — per Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: Charles Seiberling (1942), “the elder Gross” (1901), Charles Coburn (1959)
items.why: All three appear in the record with their own versions, the threshold sliding between forty and fifty — and the doctor’s fingerprints are all over it: Seiberling credited his own physician (“my doctor told me…”), and the 1901 version is credited to the surgeon “the elder Gross.” That is the signature of a proverb, not a quotation. Quote Investigator ↗
The line appears nowhere on Wikiquote’s Wright page ↗ — not in the sourced quotes, not even among the unsourced attributions.

misattribution.truthLine: Wright did say it, on the record, in the New York Times Magazine of 22 June 1958. He was passing on a doctors’ adage that had been in print since at least 1900 — and the sentence now quoted under his name is Evan Esar’s 1968 rewording of what Wright actually said. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why a doctors’ joke ended up on an architect
lead: It reads like vintage Wright — the flourish, the two-part symmetry, the licence granted to himself at exactly the age he had already passed. But the saying’s real habitat was not the drafting table. It was the consulting room. Between 1900 and the early 1950s it turns up again and again as something a physician said to a patient: in the proceedings of the American Social Science Association in 1900, in a medical journal in 1901, in the mouth of a Goodyear co-founder in 1942 quoting his doctor, in a Cleveland newspaper profile in 1943, and in a newspaper column in 1951 whose author had it from his own physician.

What Wright supplied was not the idea but the megaphone. In June 1958 a New York Times Magazine feature on people still thriving past eighty caught him sipping a single Irish whisky before dinner, and he explained himself with the adage. That is the moment a piece of half-humorous medical folk wisdom acquired a famous author — and once a saying has a famous author, nobody goes looking for the anonymous one.
detailsBody: The age discrepancy in the 1958 piece. Quote Investigator describes Wright as 89 when the article ran. Wright was in fact born on 8 June 1867 ↗, but claimed throughout his life to have been born in 1869 — which is the birth year that makes 89 the right answer in June 1958. The understatement was his own, and it is a small reminder that Wright was an unreliable narrator of his own life.

Faulkner said it too. William Faulkner of Oxford (1965) records the photographer J. R. Cofield remembering Faulkner’s version: “But a man shouldn’t fool with booze until he’s fifty; then he’s a damnfool if he doesn’t.” Two very famous men, the same borrowed adage, no contact between them required.

The threshold kept moving. Fifty in 1900, 1943, 1958 and 1965; forty in 1901, 1951 and in the actor Charles Coburn’s 1959 version. A line with a floating number is almost always a proverb rather than a quotation — nobody misremembers the punchline of a sentence they wrote themselves.
context.pull: Wright supplied the megaphone, not the idea.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator documents the full chronology: a 1792 Salem Gazette proto-version at age thirty; the earliest known matching form in the Journal of Social Science no. 38 (Dec 1900), pp. 127-28, credited to "Some one has said"; a 1901 Therapeutic Gazette version credited to "the elder Gross" at forty; 1942 Seiberling, 1943 Cleveland Plain Dealer and 1951 column instances citing doctors; Wright quoted in the New York Times Magazine of 22 June 1958 ("Life Begins at 40 (x 2)" by Arturo and Janeann Gonzalez, p. SM10) saying "A man is a fool if he drinks before he reaches the age of 50, and a fool if he doesn't afterward"; Coburn 1959; Faulkner's version in William Faulkner of Oxford (1965); and Evan Esar's 20,000 Quips and Quotes (Doubleday, 1968), p. 243, where QI states "Wright's words were slightly modified" and prints the wording that now circulates. QI concludes physicians were the nexus of dissemination and hypothesises Wright and Faulkner heard it from others.

WIST (Wish I'd Said That) carries the Wright quotation as "A man is a fool if he drinks before he reaches the age of 50, and a fool if he doesn't afterward," attributes it to Frank Lloyd Wright (1867-1959), American architect, interior designer, writer, educator, and sources it to the New York Times of 22 June 1958.
Wikiquote's Frank Lloyd Wright page does not contain this quote about drinking before or after age fifty in any section; it gives his dates as 8 June 1867 - 9 April 1959.

Wikipedia gives Frank Lloyd Wright's dates as June 8, 1867 - April 9, 1959, describes him as an American architect, designer, writer, and educator, and states that Wright claimed throughout his life that he was born in 1869.

The Internet Archive holds a scan of Journal of Social Science, Containing the Proceedings of the American Association, 1900-12: Iss 38 - the exact issue Quote Investigator cites for the earliest known matching form of the saying.
